text:
The purest treasure mortal times afford
Is spotless reputation; that away,
Men are but gilded loam or painted clay.
plain: Your good name is the real treasure. Lose it and a man is just painted clay.

text:
Mine honour is my life; both grow in one.
Take honour from me, and my life is done.
plain: Some things are the point of your life. Take them and there's no life left.

text:
That which in mean men we entitle patience
Is pale cold cowardice in noble breasts.
plain: Patience in someone with power and a duty is just cowardice by another name.

text:
Grief boundeth where it falls,
Not with the empty hollowness, but weight.
plain: Grief doesn't lie there. It bounces back with the weight of what you lost.

text:
Shorten my days thou canst with sullen sorrow,
And pluck nights from me, but not lend a morrow.
Thou canst help time to furrow me with age,
But stop no wrinkle in his pilgrimage;
plain: No one can give you back time. They can only take it faster.

text:
How long a time lies in one little word!
Four lagging winters and four wanton springs
End in a word: such is the breath of kings.
plain: A few words from the right person can rewrite years of your life.

text:
All places that the eye of heaven visits
Are to a wise man ports and happy havens.
Teach thy necessity to reason thus:
There is no virtue like necessity.
plain: To a wise man every place is a harbor. Make peace with what you can't change, and make it useful.

text:
For gnarling sorrow hath less power to bite
The man that mocks at it and sets it light.
plain: Sorrow loses its bite when you laugh at it and refuse to treat it as bigger than it is.

text:
O, who can hold a fire in his hand
By thinking on the frosty Caucasus?
Or cloy the hungry edge of appetite
By bare imagination of a feast?
Or wallow naked in December snow
By thinking on fantastic summer’s heat?
O no, the apprehension of the good
Gives but the greater feeling to the worse.
plain: You can't think your way warm. Imagining a better life only makes the real one feel worse. Act, don't just picture.

text:
My oil-dried lamp and time-bewasted light
Shall be extinct with age and endless night;
My inch of taper will be burnt and done,
And blindfold death not let me see my son.
plain: The light is burning down, and no one can add to the wick. Use it.

text:
More are men’s ends marked than their lives before.
The setting sun and music at the close,
As the last taste of sweets, is sweetest last,
Writ in remembrance more than things long past.
plain: People weigh your last act more than all the ones before. How you finish counts.
Burning too hot and too fast burns out. Pace beats a blaze.

text:
England, bound in with the triumphant sea,
Whose rocky shore beats back the envious siege
Of wat’ry Neptune, is now bound in with shame,
With inky blots and rotten parchment bonds
That England that was wont to conquer others
Hath made a shameful conquest of itself.
plain: The biggest danger to a strong thing is usually its own choices, not an outside enemy.

text:
We see the wind sit sore upon our sails,
And yet we strike not, but securely perish.
plain: People watch the storm come and still do nothing, and they perish from comfort.

text: Things past redress are now with me past care.
plain: What can't be fixed no longer needs your worry. Let it go.

text:
O, call back yesterday, bid time return,
And thou shalt have twelve thousand fighting men!
plain: You would give an army to get yesterday back. You can't, so use today.

text:
Our lands, our lives, and all are Bolingbroke’s,
And nothing can we call our own but death
And that small model of the barren earth
Which serves as paste and cover to our bones.
plain: At the end the only things that are yours are the earth you lie in. Everything else is borrowed.

text:
I live with bread like you, feel want,
Taste grief, need friends. Subjected thus,
How can you say to me I am a king?
plain: Take the title away and he eats, wants, hurts and needs friends like everyone else.

text:
My lord, wise men ne’er sit and wail their woes,
But presently prevent the ways to wail.
To fear the foe, since fear oppresseth strength,
Gives in your weakness strength unto your foe,
And so your follies fight against yourself.
plain: Wise people don't sit and wail. Fearing your enemy hands him strength and your fear fights for him.

text:
O, that I were as great
As is my grief, or lesser than my name,
Or that I could forget what I have been,
Or not remember what I must be now.
plain: His grief is bigger than he is, and he can neither forget who he was nor face who he must be.

text:
Now is this golden crown like a deep well
That owes two buckets, filling one another,
The emptier ever dancing in the air,
The other down, unseen, and full of water.
That bucket down and full of tears am I,
Drinking my griefs, whilst you mount up on high.
plain: When one person rises, someone else goes down and fills with grief. Wins are rarely clean for everyone.

text:
’Tis very true, my grief lies all within;
And these external manner of laments
Are merely shadows to the unseen grief
That swells with silence in the tortured soul.
plain: Tears and sad looks are only the surface. The real grief swells in silence inside.

text:
O, good! “Convey”? Conveyers are you all,
That rise thus nimbly by a true king’s fall.
plain: The people who profit when you fall always have friendly words for it.

text:
Learn, good soul,
To think our former state a happy dream,
From which awaked, the truth of what we are
Shows us but this.
plain: What you thought was your real life may turn out to be the dream. Waking up shows what you really are.

text:
I am sworn brother, sweet,
To grim Necessity, and he and I
Will keep a league till death.
plain: When life corners you, make necessity an ally. It will be with you to the end anyway.

text:
The love of wicked men converts to fear,
That fear to hate, and hate turns one or both
To worthy danger and deserved death.
plain: People who help you do wrong will fear you, then hate you. Loyalty bought with sin comes due.

text:
A king of beasts, indeed! If aught but beasts,
I had been still a happy king of men.
plain: If you live as a beast, you lose the one thing you had as a man.

text:
As in a theatre the eyes of men
After a well-graced actor leaves the stage,
Are idly bent on him that enters next,
Thinking his prattle to be tedious,
Even so, or with much more contempt, men’s eyes
Did scowl on gentle Richard.
plain: The crowd looks at whoever enters next. Yesterday's star is forgotten the moment he leaves the stage.

text:
I wasted time, and now doth time waste me;
For now hath time made me his numb’ring clock.
plain: He wasted his time, and now time is wasting him. Spend it while it's yours.

text:
Ha, ha! keep time! How sour sweet music is
When time is broke and no proportion kept!
So is it in the music of men’s lives.
plain: A life out of time sounds sour. Rhythm is what makes any life, or any day, work.

text:
Now is the winter of our discontent
Made glorious summer by this son of York;
And all the clouds that loured upon our house
In the deep bosom of the ocean buried.
plain: Sometimes the hard season ends. The dark clouds can go to the bottom of the sea.

text:
They that stand high have many blasts to shake them,
And if they fall they dash themselves to pieces.
plain: The higher you stand the more wind hits you, and a fall from there breaks you.

text:
Sorrow breaks seasons and reposing hours,
Makes the night morning, and the noontide night.
plain: Sorrow takes over the clock. The night feels like morning and noon feels like night.

text:
Scoffing his state and grinning at his pomp,
Allowing him a breath, a little scene,
To monarchize, be feared, and kill with looks,
Infusing him with self and vain conceit,
As if this flesh which walls about our life
Were brass impregnable; and, humoured thus,
Comes at the last, and with a little pin
Bores through his castle wall, and farewell, king!
plain: Death sits inside every crown and lets a man feel invincible just long enough, then ends it with a pin.
